title: I Am Death, Destroyer of Worlds
story:
Arjuna looked into the mouth of the universe and saw his own family entering it.

The war on the field of Kurukshetra had not yet begun, and in the pause Krishna, Arjuna's cousin, his friend, and his charioteer, had answered Arjuna's longing to see his true form. Now the form stood before him like a second sky: a thousand faces, a thousand arms, mouths blazing like the fire that waits at the end of the world, crowned and armed with mace and discus, glowing on every side. Heaven and earth, gods and beasts, everything that is, was gathered into that one body. The sun and the moon were its eyes; the fire of the world's ending was its mouth.

Arjuna saw the creator Brahma on his lotus seat, the sages and the shining serpents, the hosts called the Rudras, the Adityas, the Vasus, the Ashwins and the Maruts. He saw gods streaming into the form while others, afraid, stood with joined hands, and great sages praising it with hymns. The sight had no beginning and no end, and at the sight of it the three worlds trembled. "I can find no end of you, no middle, no beginning," Arjuna whispered, his hair standing on end.

And then he saw what the mouths were for. "The sons of Dhritarashtra, my cousins, are rushing into your terrible mouths," he cried, "and all their kings with them. Bhishma the grandsire is there, and Drona, who taught us to fight, and Karna the charioteer's son, the champion of the Kauravas, and the bravest warriors of our own side too. All of them are pouring into that flame. Some are caught between your great teeth. As rivers run to the sea, they run into you. As moths fly into a fire, they fly to their end. I can no longer find courage or peace. Be gracious to us, lord of the gods."

And out of the blaze a voice answered, the same voice that had driven his chariot, the same voice that had spoken of the soul that cannot die. "I am Death," it said. "I have grown beyond all measure, and I am destroying these worlds. These warriors are already slain. I have slain them. You need only be my instrument."

The words fell on Arjuna like a second revelation. The war he had dreaded, the killing he had refused, the kinsmen he could not bear to face, all of it had already happened, inside the will of the one who stood before him. The warriors streaming into those mouths were not about to die. They were already gone. What remained was only one question: would Arjuna be the willing instrument, or something less?

The vision blazed around him, mouths and tusks and flame, bright as a hundred suns, and Arjuna, trembling, bowed his head in the middle of that fire. He had asked to see the truth, and the truth was this: the battle was not his to begin or to refuse. It was his to serve, or his to watch in helplessness, and the whole difference between those two lay in that single choice. Still the voice waited for his answer.
reflection: The terrible form is the kindest thing Krishna could have shown him: the war Arjuna fears to cause has already happened — the warriors are already gone. His choice is not whether they die but whether he will be the willing instrument or the helpless witness, and the whole of the Gita's call to action rests on that strange, liberating knowledge.
content_note: Contains imagery of warriors being drawn into the cosmic form's flaming mouths; intense but not graphic.
next_story_tease: Then, as suddenly, the cosmic form would fold back into the charioteer's gentle shape.
hero_scene: Within the blazing cosmic form, the warriors of both armies stream like rivers into Krishna's flaming, tusk-fierce mouths, while a small Arjuna stands before the vision with joined hands, his hair standing on end.
